title: Rapid stump-and-fix demo sprint
summary: Internal rapid-fire session to run through tough demo scenarios for Polaris Commerce. Action items assigned for follow-ups and a technical deep-dive scheduled.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-11
Start time: 2:00 PM PST
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Product), Leah Ortiz (Solutions), Samir Patel (Polaris Head of ML), Jordan Lee (Eng Mgr), Alyssa Grant (Product Lead), Tom Briggs (Security)

Summary: Rapid 'stump the demo' internal session; run through tough customer questions, practice concise answers, and surface follow-ups.

00:00:05 Maya Chen: All right everyone. Thanks for carving out time. The plan is quick — we run three "stump me" scenarios from Polaris, Carlos will demo quick failover bits, and we practice tight rebuttals. Keep answers short, call out follow-ups. Ready?
00:00:22 Carlos Rivera: Yep, ready. I'll flag if I need to drop to a whiteboard.
00:00:28 Samir Patel: Cool. I can kick off with the first tough one — cost. They asked, "why would we pay for dedicated when the open models are cheaper on standard infra?"
00:00:39 Maya Chen: Good. Short answer first, then meat. Short: Dedicated gives predictable latency and isolation you can't get on noisy multi-tenant hosts — important for SLAs. But let's say that again with numbers.
00:00:56 Carlos Rivera: Right — add the unit economics. Example: for the 2k QPS pattern Polaris described, bursty nights, the per-token cost on hosted with variable latencies can be 20–40% more when you account for tail latencies and retries. If you amortize reserved capacity, per-token drops and latencies tighten.
00:01:18 Jordan Lee: Quick interruption — that 20–40% feels hand-wavy. Do you have a benchmark we can show quickly?
00:01:26 Maya Chen: Yeah we should call out a reference: the benchmark sheet we shared — the northbound table where a 4-GPU dedicated pool averaged 20ms p50 vs 120ms on shared during storms. We can drop that on the spot, but don't promise exact numbers without a pilot.
00:01:44 Samir Patel: Okay, but if we're using quantized open models, cost delta narrows. How do you handle model parity and quality?
00:01:54 Carlos Rivera: Good point — quality is workload dependent. Our Optimize tool suggests quantization profiles per model and gives sample regen metrics. In practice, for retrieval-augmented generation tasks we saw negligible degradations with int8 on a tuned profile. But we put the caveat in: run your evals — we'll help instrument that.
00:02:18 Alyssa Grant: When you say "Optimize tool" do you mean Redwood Optimize in the console?
00:02:27 Priya Nair: Yes, that's our Optimize surface in Console. It gives batch/quant suggestions and shows token cost delta plus flagged regressions against eval sets. I can pull a quick screenshot, but not in this sprint.
00:02:39 Tom Briggs: For security folks — how does KMS and key management work with Dedicated vs Private? We need full control over keys and audit logs.
00:02:50 Carlos Rivera: For Dedicated you can use customer-managed keys via KMS integration and HSM if required. For Private (VPC/on-prem) the control plane is customer-managed; logs are sent to your SIEM — we have examples for Splunk and Sumo.
00:03:04 Tom Briggs: Example please — how long are audit logs retained?
00:03:08 Priya Nair: Out of the box, platform retention is 30 days, but enterprises can purchase extended retention or ship logs to their S3 with retention policies — typical enterprise configs run 1–7 years depending on regs. We'll confirm Polaris' reg needs and map.
00:03:25 Maya Chen: Okay next stump scenario — latency-critical path. Polaris says checkout latency must be <200ms end-to-end for personalization. How do we answer?
00:03:36 Carlos Rivera: We break it into pieces. 1) model: pick a low-latency variant or a distilled checkpoint; 2) runtime: batch sizes tuned to keep p95 under threshold; 3) caching: prefix and KV cache for session tokens; 4) routing: colocate inference region with frontend; 5) fallback: have a scaled-down faster model to keep SLOs.
00:04:01 Jordan Lee: The routing bit — can you route by latency SLA automatically? We need policy-based routing with geos.
00:04:08 Carlos Rivera: Yes — smart routing policies can prefer low-latency pool in region, then fall back to cost pool. We call out that cross-region fallbacks add latency; prefer pre-warming or bursts in dedicated pools for known peak windows.
00:04:23 Samir Patel: When you say "fallback to cost pool" what's the observable difference? Does the SDK surface fallback reasons?
00:04:30 Leah Ortiz: The console will show per-request routing and the token-level cost/breakdown; we also emit a routing tag in the trace so you can filter by fallback reason. Slightly noisy in transcripts — but it's there.
00:04:46 Maya Chen: Quick role-play — customer's AE says "we can't justify Dedicated in Q1." How do you close or route to pilot?
00:04:55 Carlos Rivera: Offer a pilot: small reserved pool with auto-burst credits, clear success metrics (p95 < X, cost per 1K tokens < Y). Propose a 4–8 week pilot with a rollback clause. Show them the cost model.
00:05:10 Alyssa Grant: What's the minimum commit? We need to know numbers.
00:05:14 Maya Chen: Don't give fixed numbers in this meeting. Say: "we can propose a pilot tailored to your traffic shape — we'll size conservatively and show projected amortized cost." Offer to follow up with a tailored quote.
00:05:26 Samir Patel: Okay next: uptime and graceful degradation. If the big model fails, do we have automatic fallbacks to smaller models?
00:05:34 Carlos Rivera: Yes — we have rollout policies, canary, A/B, and automatic fallback chains. You can pin versions. In Dedicated you can configure standby pools with lighter models.
00:05:47 Jordan Lee: Can we set custom regen logic? For example, if confidence below threshold, fall back to retrieval or canned templates?
00:05:55 Priya Nair: We're adding conditional function calling hooks — but today we recommend the app layer handle retrieval/skip logic; we can demonstrate a pattern. That's a follow-up with engineering.
00:06:10 Maya Chen: Good. We'll note that as an action item: show example pattern with function hooks.
00:06:16 [00:06:20] (Brief side conversation - Leah to Carlos about demo notes)
00:06:40 Maya Chen: All right Carlos, do the 10-minute failover demo you prepared — quick narration please.
00:06:45 Carlos Rivera: Sure. I'll share screen — (audio) I'm going to simulate high latency on the primary pool then show automatic route to standby. Okay, screen shared. Starting request flood — see tail p95 climbing to ~350ms, then route triggered, fallback model responds under 60ms and error rates drop.
00:07:12 Jordan Lee: That routing tag — can we see it in traces with request id?
00:07:16 Carlos Rivera: Yep, trace includes pool_id and route_reason, and you can correlate with request id in the SDK logs.
00:07:22 Samir Patel: The demo looked scripted — in a PoC will you simulate real traffic from our instance?
00:07:28 Carlos Rivera: For PoC we can ingest a replay of production traffic to get realistic patterns. We'll run your trace for a week and build the right config.
00:07:35 Maya Chen: Quick objection handling practice: "If we run on-prem, dev velocity suffers and ops complexity increases." How do you keep it concise?
00:07:45 Priya Nair: Say: "On-prem has tradeoffs; we provide an opinionated packaging and runbook, and you can choose hybrid where control plane is Redwood-hosted but inference runs in your VPC to balance velocity and control."
00:07:58 Alyssa Grant: Does hybrid still allow KMS control?
00:08:02 Priya Nair: Yes — KMS keys can be customer-managed and never leave your VPC.
00:08:08 Samir Patel: Pricing question — how do you charge for private vs hosted? Is there a platform fee?
00:08:15 Maya Chen: Typically private has a platform fee based on deployment size plus usage. We'll outline options in the quote. Don't low-ball; highlight value.
00:08:26 [00:08:30] (Short laughter)
00:08:39 Maya Chen: Last stump scenario — compliance. Tom, give us the tough one.
00:08:43 Tom Briggs: We need doxxed data handling for EU customers, and a SCORM-type evidence trail for audits. Who owns redaction and PII handling?
00:08:53 Carlos Rivera: We provide redaction libraries and edge filters as patterns. For high-risk PII we recommend pre-send tokenization in the client and post-response scrubbers. Also the private deployment can be air-gapped and we support offline evals. For audit trails, audit logs + immutable S3 sinks with object versioning cover regulatory-proofing.
00:09:20 Tom Briggs: And SOC2?
00:09:22 Priya Nair: We're SOC2 compliant — details in the security pack. We'll send the security deck and the attestation.
00:09:28 Maya Chen: Okay final rapid round: each of us does a 30-second 'closing pitch' to Polaris — go. Carlos?
00:09:36 Carlos Rivera: Quick pitch: Redwood gives predictable inference at scale with production-grade controls — routing, caching, and failover. We make it practical to hit latency SLAs while optimizing cost.
00:09:46 Maya Chen: Maya: Redwood makes it easy to migrate from dev experiments to production with built-in rollouts and cost controls; we help you measure impact not just performance.
00:09:56 Priya Nair: Priya: With Optimize and eval hooks, we catch quality regressions early so your product owners sleep at night — and we tune quantization per workload.
00:10:06 Samir Patel: Short ask: Show us a pilot plan with clear metrics. If that exists, we'll greenlight the pilot.
00:10:12 Maya Chen: Noted. We'll come back with a pilot pack.
00:10:18 Jordan Lee: And include a quick runbook for troubleshooting; my infra team wants to know when to escalate to Redwood SEs.
00:10:25 Maya Chen: We'll include escalation and runbook.
00:10:30 Alyssa Grant: Great. Thanks everyone.
00:10:34 Maya Chen: Wrap-up: action items we agreed — Carlos build failover demo (due 2/18), Priya send SOC2/KMS page (2/14), Maya send objection cheat-sheet and pilot outline (2/13). We'll propose 2/18 for the infra deep-dive. Anything else?
00:10:52 Tom Briggs: Please also include log retention options and an example SLA.
00:10:57 Maya Chen: Got it.
00:11:05 (some background chatter as participants drop off)

[Note: rest of conversation was quick followups and deliberation between AE/SE about refining slides and ensuring Polaris-specific examples; session was 75 minutes total including prep/screen share. The transcript above captures the main recorded content; we omitted some internal stage directions.]

End of meeting.
